key_gap: The AI matched every checkable number (min-capacity 80/hr before, 100/hr after A; B/C/D/E rejected) and named the same post-lift constraint tie (S2/S3 at 100/hr), but it reached the answer by enumerating and pricing all five programs, where the pure constraint pass short-circuits with one structural rule (investment off the constraint cannot change the line's output), and its two best insights — the WIP-buffer signature as the empirical constraint locator and the constraint-movement step — came from the verify machinery rather than the initial frame; the human named both before any option math.
learning_signal: For serial throughput problems the pure constraint pass is faster and equally correct: read the capacity chain as min(), locate the constraint empirically by its WIP signature (work accumulates only just upstream of the slowest stage), exploit it free (recover starvation), subordinate everything else to it, invest only in the minimum element, and after any lift repeat the pass (the constraint moves — after A the min became a tie). The AI's exhaustive option enumeration was redundant work the min-element rule eliminates.
suggested_improvement: Add a WHAT-stage default frame for serial-capacity problems: compute min(stage rates) and demand first; pre-filter any proposed investment with the rule 'an option that does not touch the current min element cannot change throughput' before pricing it; require an explicit 'where does the constraint move after this lift?' answer for any accepted option; and treat the WIP-buffer signature (where inventory accumulates) as the first-class empirical locator of the constraint, stated before the capacity table is read.

key_gap: Pure bottleneck thinking presupposed the org-chart serial flow as fixed structure: it declared human adjudication the constraint (400 < 420), dismissed the idle 250/day automated engine as a 'side channel, not part of the flow,' and treated the constraint as static over the investment horizon — missing both the routing-policy artifact (re-routing low-touch claims clears the backlog at zero capex; the system is demand-constrained, not capacity-constrained) and the mix shift that dissolves the constraint before the hires land (month-6 high-touch ≈ 353 < 400), making the $1.2M/yr plan zero-return.
learning_signal: The question 'which stage binds?' presupposes the flow structure. Before identifying any constraint, verify the structure is actually serial and fixed: inventory all processing resources including idle/parallel ones, check whether routing policy forces work through a station that a policy change could bypass, and stress-test the constraint at the investment's completion horizon — demand and mix can move it, and in this case dissolved it. Apparent constraints that vanish under a policy change are artifacts, and capital keyed to them is waste.
suggested_improvement: In WHAT/WHY for capacity diagnoses, add a mandatory structure check before constraint identification: (a) enumerate every processing resource, including idle and parallel ones, regardless of the org chart; (b) compute the flow under the current routing policy and under the best policy alternative; (c) if a policy change alone brings every resource below 100% utilization, classify the system as policy/demand-constrained and gate any capacity investment behind a re-check at the investment's completion horizon, with a quantified trigger threshold (here: high-touch volume > 400/day, share > ~85%) rather than a standing commitment.
